draft.alt: The Unified Soil Classification table: 15 soil groups (GW to Pt), with field and lab identification methods, descriptions, and a plasticity chart.
draft.long:
Column headings: 1 and 2, Major divisions. 3, Group symbols. 4, Typical names. 5, Field identification procedures (excluding particles larger than 3 in. and basing fractions on estimated weights). 6, Information required for describing soils. 7, Laboratory classification criteria.

COARSE-GRAINED SOILS. More than half of material is larger than No. 200 sieve size. (The No. 200 sieve size is about the smallest visible to the naked eye.)

Gravels: more than half of coarse fraction is larger than No. 4 sieve size. (For visual classification, the 1/4-in. size may be used as equivalent to the No. 4 sieve size.)
Clean gravels (little or no fines):
- GW. Well-graded gravels, gravel-sand mixture, little or no fines. Field: Wide range in grain size and substantial amounts of all intermediate particle sizes. Lab: Cu = D60 / D10 greater than 4; Cc = (D30)² / (D10 × D60) between 1 and 3.
- GP. Poorly graded gravels or gravel-sand mixture, little or no fines. Field: Predominantly one size or a range of sizes with some intermediate sizes missing. Lab: Not meeting all gradation requirements for GW.
Gravels with fines (appreciable amount of fines):
- GM. Silty gravels, gravel and silt mixtures. Field: Nonplastic fines or fines with low plasticity (for identification procedures see ML below). Lab: Atterberg limits below "A" line or P1 less than 4.
- GC. Clayey gravels, gravel and clay mixtures. Field: Plastic fines (for identification procedures see CL below). Lab: Atterberg limits above "A" line with P1 greater than 7.
- Lab note for GM and GC: Above "A" line with P1 between 4 and 7 are borderline cases requiring use of dual symbols.

Sands: more than half of coarse fraction is smaller than No. 4 sieve size.
Clean sand (little or no fines):
- SW. Well-graded sands, gravelly sands, little or no fines. Field: Wide range in grain size and substantial amounts of all intermediate particle sizes. Lab: Cu = D60 / D10 greater than 6; Cc = (D30)² / (D10 × D60) between 1 and 3.
- SP. Poorly graded sands or gravelly sands, little or no fines. Field: Predominantly one size or a range of sizes with some intermediate sizes missing. Lab: Not meeting all gradation requirements for SW.
Sands with fines (appreciable amount of fines):
- SM. Silty sands, sand-silt mixtures. Field: Nonplastic fines or fines with low plasticity (for identification procedures see ML below). Lab: Atterberg limits above "A" line or P1 less than 4.
- SC. Clayey sands, sand-clay mixtures. Field: Plastic fines (for identification procedures see CL below). Lab: Atterberg limits above "A" line with P1 greater than 7.
- Lab note for SM and SC: Limits plotting in hatched zone with P1 between 4 and 7 are borderline cases requiring use of dual symbols.

Information required for describing coarse-grained soils (column 6): For undisturbed soils add information on stratification, degree of compactness, cementation, moisture condition, and drainage characteristics. Give typical name; indicate approximate percentages of sand and gravel, maximum size; angularity, surface condition, and hardness of the coarse grains; local or geologic name and other pertinent descriptive information; and symbol in parentheses. Example: Silty sand, gravelly; about 20% hard, angular gravel particles 1/2-in. maximum size; rounded and subangular sand grains, coarse to fine; about 15% nonplastic fines with low dry strength; well compacted and moist in place; alluvial sand; (SM).

Lab criteria for coarse-grained soils, side text (column 7): Use grain-size curve in identifying the fractions as given under field identification. Determine percentage of gravel and sand from grain-size curve. Depending on percentage of fine (fraction smaller than No. 200 sieve size) coarse-grained soils are classified as follows: Less than 5%: GW, GP, SW, SP. More than 12%: GM, GC, SM, SC. 5% to 12%: Borderline cases requiring use of dual symbols.

FINE-GRAINED SOILS. More than half of material is smaller than No. 200 sieve size. Field identification procedure on fraction smaller than No. 40 sieve size, in three columns: Dry strength (crushing characteristics); Dilatancy (reaction to shaking); Toughness (consistency near PL).

Silts and clays, liquid limit is less than 50:
- ML. Inorganic silts and very fine sands, rock flour, silty or clayey fine sands or clayey silts with slight plasticity. Dry strength: None to slight. Dilatancy: Quick to slow. Toughness: None.
- CL. Inorganic clays of low to medium plasticity, gravelly clays, sandy clays, silty clays, lean clays. Dry strength: Medium to high. Dilatancy: None to very slow. Toughness: Medium.
- OL. Organic silts and organic silty clays of low plasticity. Dry strength: Slight to medium. Dilatancy: Slow. Toughness: Slight.
Silts and clays, liquid limit is greater than 50:
- MH. Inorganic silts, micaceous or diatomaceous fine sandy or silty soils, elastic silts. Dry strength: Slight to medium. Dilatancy: Slow to none. Toughness: Slight to medium.
- CH. Inorganic clays of high plasticity, fat clays. Dry strength: High to very high. Dilatancy: None. Toughness: High.
- OH. Organic clays of medium to high plasticity, organic silts. Dry strength: Medium to high. Dilatancy: None to very slow. Toughness: Slight to medium.

HIGHLY ORGANIC SOILS:
- Pt. Peat and other highly organic soils. Field: Readily identified by color, odor, spongy feel and frequently by fibrous texture.

Information required for describing fine-grained soils (column 6): For undisturbed soils add information on structure, stratification, consistency in undisturbed and remolded states, moisture and drainage conditions. Give typical name; indicate degree and character of plasticity; amount and maximum size of coarse grains; color in wet condition; odor, if any; local or geologic name and other pertinent descriptive information; and symbol in parentheses. Example: Clayey silt, brown; slightly plastic; small percentage of fine sand; numerous vertical root holes; firm and dry in place; loess; (ML).

Liquid Limit Plasticity Chart, for laboratory classification of fine-grained soils (bottom of column 7): a graph with Plasticity Index on the vertical axis, 0 to 60 (with marks at 4 and 7), and a horizontal axis from 0 to 100. A straight line labeled 'A Line' rises from about 20 on the horizontal axis to the top right corner. CL and CH are above the line; ML and 'OH & MH' are below it; a small CL-ML zone sits low on the left between 4 and 7. A note in the chart reads: Comparing Soils at Equal Liquid Limit Toughness and Dry Strength Increase with Increasing Plasticity Index.

Notes under the table: 1. Boundary classifications: Soils possessing characteristics of two groups are designed by combinations of group symbols. For example GM-GC, well-graded gravel-sand mixture with clay binder. 2. All sieve sizes on this chart are U.S. standard. 3. Adopted by Corps of Engineers and Bureau of Reclamation, January 1952. A code '032058C' is printed in the bottom right corner.
draft.unsure: Small print throughout. The table prints 'P1' where the plasticity index (PI) is meant; I kept 'P1'. The subscripts on Cu and Cc are blurry. The SM row reads 'Atterberg limits above "A" line or P1 less than 4' in the picture (the GM row says 'below'); I wrote what is printed. The fraction in '1/4-in. size' and '1/2-in. maximum size' is tiny and may be misread. The note inside the plasticity chart is blurry; it was checked on a zoomed copy and reads as given. The chart's horizontal axis has no visible label. Which rows the two column-6 blocks cover is my reading of the layout.

draft.alt: Chart of depth below ground (0 to 50 feet) against SPT N60 blows per foot, with limit lines marking where liquefaction evaluation is required.
draft.long:
Title across the top axis: "SPT N60 : blows / foot", running from 0 to 30 in steps of 5. Left axis: "Depth below Ground Surface : feet", running from 0 at the top down to 50 in steps of 5.

Two nearly straight lines slope slightly to the right as depth grows:
- The line marked "II/III" (thinner) starts at about N60 = 16 at depth 0 and reaches about N60 = 20 at 50 feet.
- The line marked "IV" (thicker) starts at about N60 = 18 at depth 0 and reaches about N60 = 23 at 50 feet.

The area to the left of the lines is labeled "Liquefaction evaluation required". The area to the right is labeled "Liquefaction evaluation not required".

Key: "Limit Lines": thin line = "Risk Category II/III"; thick line = "Risk Category IV".

"Notes:
1) Diagram is applicable only to soils below the groundwater table.
2) N60 is the standard penetration resistance normalized to an energy of 60 percent efficiency.
3) See Table 1604.5 for Risk Category definitions.
4) Risk Category I structures are exempt from liquefaction assessment."
draft.unsure: The line end points (about 16 to 20, and about 18 to 23) are read by eye from the chart, not from printed numbers.

draft.alt: Graph for sizing a masonry chimney flue from the fireplace opening area and the chimney height.
draft.long:
Horizontal axis: Height, measured from floor of combustion chamber to top of flue (ft), from 13 to 25.
Right vertical axis: Fireplace opening area (sq. in.), from 200 to 3000 in steps of 200.
Left side: Minimum cross-sectional area (square inches), in two columns, one for round flues and one for square or rectangular flues.

There are eight curves, one for each flue size. Each curve rises from left to right, so a taller chimney lets the same flue serve a larger fireplace opening. From top to bottom, with the fireplace opening area read off the right axis (approximate):

1. Round flue 224 sq. in., or square or rectangular flue 269 sq. in.: about 2,150 at 13 ft, reaching 3,000 at about 22 ft.
2. Round 187, or square or rectangular 214: about 1,800 at 13 ft, about 2,850 at 25 ft.
3. Round 140, or square or rectangular 168: about 1,375 at 13 ft, about 2,200 at 25 ft.
4. Round 110, or square or rectangular 124: about 1,075 at 13 ft, about 1,725 at 25 ft.
5. Round 76, or square or rectangular 91: about 750 at 13 ft, about 1,225 at 25 ft.
6. Round 70, or square or rectangular 82: about 600 at 13 ft, about 975 at 25 ft.
7. Round 53, or square or rectangular 58: about 450 at 13 ft, about 750 at 25 ft.
8. Round 32, or square or rectangular 37: about 300 at 13 ft, about 475 at 25 ft.
draft.unsure: The fireplace opening values for each curve are my estimates read from the graph, not printed numbers. The flue areas (224/269 and so on) are printed and clear.

draft.alt: Table 11-1, Unified Soil Classification (including identification and description): a table of 15 soil groups with a plasticity chart.
draft.long:
Title: TABLE 11-1 UNIFIED SOIL CLASSIFICATION (Including Identification and Description).

Column headings: (1, 2) Major Divisions; (3) Group Symbols; (4) Typical Names; (5) Field Identification Procedures (excluding particles larger than 3 in. and basing fractions on estimated weights); (6) Information Required for Describing Soils; (7) Laboratory Classification Criteria.

A note down the side of the Major Divisions column reads: The No. 200 sieve size is about the smallest visible to the naked eye.

COARSE-GRAINED SOILS (more than half of material is larger than No. 200 sieve size).

Gravels (more than half of coarse fraction is larger than No. 4 sieve size). A side note reads: For visual classification, the 1/4-in. size may be used as equivalent to the No. 4 sieve size.
Clean gravels (little or no fines):
- GW. Typical names: Well-graded gravels, gravel-sand mixture, little or no fines. Field identification: Wide range in grain size and substantial amounts of all intermediate particle sizes.
- GP. Typical names: Poorly graded gravels or gravel-sand mixture, little or no fines. Field identification: Predominantly one size or a range of sizes with some intermediate sizes missing.
Gravels with fines (appreciable amount of fines):
- GM. Typical names: Silty gravels, gravel-and-silt mixtures. Field identification: Nonplastic fines or fines with low plasticity (for identification procedures see ML below).
- GC. Typical names: Clayey gravels, gravel and clay mixtures. Field identification: Plastic fines (for identification procedures see CL below).

Sands (more than half of coarse fraction is smaller than No. 4 sieve size).
Clean sands (little or no fines):
- SW. Typical names: Well-graded sands, gravelly sands, little or no fines. Field identification: Wide range in grain size and substantial amounts of all intermediate particle sizes.
- SP. Typical names: Poorly graded sands or gravelly sands, little or no fines. Field identification: Predominantly one size or a range of sizes with some intermediate sizes missing.
Sands with fines (appreciable amount of fines):
- SM. Typical names: Silty sands, sand-silt mixtures. Field identification: Nonplastic fines or fines with low plasticity (for identification procedures see ML below).
- SC. Typical names: Clayey sands, sand clay mixtures. Field identification: Plastic fines (for identification procedures see CL below).

Information required for describing coarse-grained soils: For undisturbed soils add information on stratification, degree of compactness, cementation, moisture condition, and drainage characteristics. Give typical name; indicate approximate percentages of sand and gravel, maximum size; angularity, surface condition, and hardness of the coarse grains; local or geologic name and other pertinent descriptive information; and symbol in parentheses. Example: Silty sand, gravelly; about 20% hard, angular gravel particles [illegible]-in. maximum size; rounded and subangular sand grains, coarse to fine; about 15% nonplastic fines with low dry strength; well compacted and moist in place; alluvial sand; (SM).

FINE-GRAINED SOILS (more than half of material is smaller than No. 200 sieve size).
Field identification for these groups is headed: Identification Procedure on Fraction Smaller than No. 40 Sieve Size, with three columns: Dry Strength (crushing characteristics); Dilatancy (reaction to shaking); Toughness (consistency near PL).

Silts and clays, liquid limit is less than 50:
- ML. Typical names: Inorganic silts and very fine sands, rock flour, silty or clayey fine sands or clayey silts with slight plasticity. Dry strength: None to slight. Dilatancy: Quick to slow. Toughness: None.
- CL. Typical names: Inorganic clays of low to medium plasticity, gravelly clays, sandy clays, silty clays, lean clays. Dry strength: Medium to high. Dilatancy: None to very slow. Toughness: Medium.
- OL. Typical names: Organic silts and organic silty clays of low plasticity. Dry strength: Slight to medium. Dilatancy: Slow. Toughness: Slight.

Silts and clays, liquid limit is greater than 50:
- MH. Typical names: Inorganic silts, micaceous or diatomaceous fine sandy or silty soils, elastic silts. Dry strength: Slight to medium. Dilatancy: Slow to none. Toughness: Slight to medium.
- CH. Typical names: Inorganic clays of high plasticity, fat clays. Dry strength: High to very high. Dilatancy: None. Toughness: High.
- OH. Typical names: Organic clays of medium to high plasticity, organic silts. Dry strength: Medium to high. Dilatancy: None to very slow. Toughness: Slight to medium.

Highly organic soils:
- Pt. Typical names: Peat and other highly organic soils. Field identification: Readily identified by color, odor, spongy feel and frequently by fibrous texture.

Information required for describing fine-grained soils: For undisturbed soils add information on structure, stratification, consistency in undisturbed and remolded states, moisture and drainage conditions. Give typical name; indicate degree and character of plasticity, amount and maximum size of coarse grains, color in wet condition; odor, if any; local or geologic name and other pertinent descriptive information, and symbol in parentheses. Example: Clayey silt, brown; slightly plastic; small percentage of fine sand; numerous vertical root holes; firm and dry in place; loess; (ML).

LABORATORY CLASSIFICATION CRITERIA.
A note down the side reads: Use grain-size curve in identifying the fractions as given under field identification. Determine percentage of gravel and sand from grain-size curve. Depending on percentage of fine (fraction smaller than No. 200 sieve size) coarse-grained soils are classified as follows: Less than 5%: GW, GP, SW, SP. More than 12%: GM, GC, SM, SC. 5% to 12%: Borderline cases requiring use of dual symbols.
- GW: Cu = D60 / D10, greater than 4. Cc = (D30) squared / (D10 x D60), between 1 and 3.
- GP: Not meeting all gradation requirements for GW.
- GM: Atterberg limits below "A" line or PI less than 4.
- GC: Atterberg limits above "A" line with PI greater than 7.
- For GM and GC: Above "A" line with PI between 4 and 7 are borderline cases requiring use of dual symbols.
- SW: Cu = D60 / D10, greater than 6. Cc = (D30) squared / (D10 x D60), between 1 and 3.
- SP: Not meeting all gradation requirements for SW.
- SM: Atterberg limits above "A" line or PI less than 4.
- SC: Atterberg limits above "A" line with PI greater than 7.
- For SM and SC: Limits plotting in hatched zone with PI between 4 and 7 are borderline cases requiring use of dual symbols.

PLASTICITY CHART (for laboratory classification of fine grained soils). A graph with Liquid Limit across the bottom, from 0 to 100, and Plasticity Index up the side, from 0 to 60, with marks at 4 and 7. A straight line labeled "A Line" rises from liquid limit 20 at plasticity index 0 to the top right corner of the chart. Labels on the chart: CH above the line at the upper right; CL above the line at a liquid limit of about 30 to 35; "OH & MH" below the line at a liquid limit of about 60 to 65; ML below the line at about 30; CL-ML on a shaded band between plasticity index 4 and 7 at liquid limits of about 10 to 28. A note on the chart reads: Comparing Soils at Equal Liquid Limit: Toughness and Dry Strength Increase with Increasing Plasticity Index.

Footnotes:
(1) Boundary classifications: Soils possessing characteristics of two groups are designated by combinations of group symbols. For example GM-GC, well-graded gravel-sand mixture with clay binder.
(2) All sieve sizes on this chart are U.S. standard.
(3) Adopted by Corps of Engineers and Bureau of Reclamation, January 1952.

draft.alt: Table 3-4 (continued): required fire-resistance ratings in hours for Construction Group II (combustible), classes II-A through II-E.
draft.long:
Table 3-4, Construction Classifications (continued). Construction Group II, Combustible. Required fire-resistance ratings of construction elements in hours, based on the test procedures of reference standard RS 3-1. Key: N.P. = Not permitted. N.L. = No limit. The key also has an entry "Noncombustible materials".

Columns: Class II-A, Class II-B, Class II-C, Class II-D, Class II-E. For exterior walls, each class has two values: Rating in Hrs. and Ext. Open'g (notes a, b).

Exterior walls with an exterior separation of 3'-0" or less:
- Bearing: rating 2 for II-A, 2 for II-B, 2 for II-C, 2 for II-D, 2 for II-E.
- Non-bearing (note f): rating 2 for all five classes.
- Exterior openings: N.P. for all five classes.

Exterior walls with an exterior separation of more than 3'-0" but less than 15'-0":
- Bearing: II-A 2, II-B 2, II-C 2, II-D 1, II-E 1.
- Non-bearing (note f): II-A 2, II-B 2, II-C 2, II-D 1, II-E 1.
- Exterior openings: II-A, II-B and II-C 3 1/3% protected; II-D and II-E 6 2/3%.

Exterior walls with an exterior separation of 15'-0" or more but less than 30'-0":
- Bearing: II-A 2, II-B 2, II-C 2, II-D 1, II-E 0.
- Non-bearing (note f): II-A 2, II-B 2, II-C 2, II-D 1, II-E 0.
- Exterior openings: II-A, II-B and II-C 3 1/3%; II-D and II-E N.L.

Exterior walls with an exterior separation of 30'-0" or more:
- Bearing: II-A 1, II-B 1 1/2, II-C 1 1/2, II-D 1, II-E 0.
- Non-bearing (note f): 0 for all five classes.
- Exterior openings: N.L. for all five classes.

Interior bearing walls and bearing partitions: II-A 2, II-B 1, II-C 0, II-D 1, II-E 0.

Enclosure of vertical exits (note e), exit passageways, hoistways and shafts: II-A 2, II-B 2, II-C 1 (note i), II-D 1 (note i), II-E 1.

Fire divisions and fire separations: See Article 5 (all classes).

Columns, girders, trusses (other than roof trusses) and framing (note k):
- Supporting one floor: II-A see section 27-623, II-B 1, II-C 0 or 1 (note j), II-D 1, II-E 0.
- Supporting more than one floor: II-A see section 27-623, II-B 1, II-C 0 or 1 (note j), II-D 1, II-E 0.

Structural members supporting a wall: Same as required fire resistance of wall supported, but not less than rating required for member by the class of construction (all classes).

Floor construction including beams: II-A see section 27-623, II-B 1, II-C 0 or 1 (note j), II-D 1, II-E 0.

Roof construction including beams, trusses and framing, including arches, domes, shells, cable supported roofs and roof decks (note h):
- 15'-0" or less in height above floor to lowest member: II-A see section 27-623, II-B 3/4, II-C 0, II-D 3/4, II-E 0.
- 15'-0" to 20'-0" in height above floor to lowest member: II-A see section 27-623, II-B 3/4, II-C 0, II-D 3/4, II-E 0.
- 20'-0" or more in height above floor to lowest member: II-A see section 27-623, II-B 3/4, II-C 0, II-D 3/4, II-E 0.

draft.alt: Two graphs of ceramic fiber blanket thickness needed against panel thickness, for 1 inch and 3/8 inch joints, plus a joint detail and line key.

Bottom graph, "3/8 INCH WIDTH," vertical axis 0 to 3 inches. Approximate readings: 1 hr. solid falls from about 1.5 at 3.3 inches to 0 at about 4.2 inches; 1 hr. dashed from about 0.5 at 3 inches to 0 at about 3.7. 2 hr. solid falls from about 2 at 4.7 inches to about 0.5 at 5.3 inches; 2 hr. dashed from about 1.6 at 3.5 inches to about 0.3 at 4.3. 3 hr. solid falls from about 2 at 5.8 inches to about 0.6 at 6.5; 3 hr. dashed from about 2.2 at 4.2 inches to about 0.5 at 5.3. 4 hr. solid falls from about 1.8 at 6.8 inches to about 0.5 at 7.6; 4 hr. dashed from about 1.7 at 5.4 inches to about 0.5 at 6.

Dimension C is the depth of the blanket, PANEL THICKNESS is the full depth of the panel, and JOINT WIDTH is the gap between the panels.

draft.alt: Three plan diagrams of panel layouts on a diaphragm, showing load directions for Cases 1 through 6.
draft.long:
Three rectangles side by side. Each is a top view of a diaphragm covered with panels, with part of the panels cut away at the upper right to show the framing and blocking underneath. Left diagram: the load from the top is "CASE 1" and the load from the left is "CASE 3". Panels are laid in rows with their long sides running left to right, and the end joints are staggered from row to row. Labels: "Blocking typical, if used" (pointing into the cutaway) and "Continuous panel joints" (pointing to a joint line that runs left to right).

Panels are laid in rows with their long sides running up and down, and the joints are staggered from row to row. Labels: "Framing typical" (pointing into the cutaway) and "Diaphragm boundary" (pointing to the lower left edges).

Right diagram: the load from the top is "CASE 6" and the load from the left is "CASE 5". Panels are laid in a grid, so the joints line up in both directions. Label: "Continuous panel joints" (pointing to joint lines).

Key at the bottom left: "Framing" is a solid thin line. "Blocking" is a dotted line.

Each has four curves labeled 1 hr., 2 hr., 3 hr. and 4 hr., all sloping down to the right, with 1 hr. lowest and 4 hr. highest. The 1 hr. curve starts at about 1 inch of board on a 1 inch slab and reaches 0 at a slab of roughly 2.5 to 3 inches.
